t: Designing for Users: UX and Accessibility
l: Hello and welcome to Mr Butler's Digital Technology podcast. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's topic is Designing for Users: U X and Accessibility.
This one is all about people. Not how to make an app work, but how to make it work for the people who use it.

We'll cover user-centred design, finding out what users need, personas, user stories, usability principles, wireframes and prototypes, accessibility, inclusive design, testing, and development cycles like waterfall and agile.
And at the end we'll follow a real-style project: redesigning a school canteen ordering website.
Right. Conor's confession time. Aoife, I pushed a door this morning that said pull.
Classic. But here's the thing. In design, that's usually not your fault. It's the door's fault.
I'll take that. So what is user-centred design?
User-centred design means the needs of the users come first, at every stage. You find out who they are, what they need, and how they behave, and you test your ideas with real people.
And there are three words designers use all the time. Usability is how easy it is to use a product to get a job done.
User experience, or U X, is how the whole experience feels. Quick and pleasant, or frustrating.
And the user interface, or U I, is the bit you see and touch. The screens, buttons, menus and icons.
The big idea is this. A product can work perfectly and still fail its users. So don't just ask, does it work? Ask, who does it work for?
Like a car park machine that only takes payment through a phone app. It works, if you've a smartphone, signal and battery. If you don't, you're stuck.
Exactly. And products fail users when the designer designs for themselves, guesses instead of asking, adds too many features, uses confusing words, or never tests with real people.
Which brings us to finding out what users need. The people a product is for are called the target audience.
Collecting information yourself, straight from users, is called primary research. There are three main methods.
Interviews. You talk to one person at a time and ask open questions. You get lots of detail, and the reasons why, but it's slow.
Surveys, or questionnaires. Lots of people, quick answers, easy to turn into charts. But the answers are short.
And observation. You watch people actually doing the task. Because what people say and what they do are often different.
A pupil might tell a survey they always read the menu. Then you watch the queue, and they just point at whatever their friend is having.
Guilty again. Then designers sum up their research in personas.
A persona is a realistic, made-up character who represents one group of users. Name, age, goals, frustrations, the devices they use.
Like Orla, twelve, Year 8, gets the bus from Lisnaskea, has an old Android phone with a cracked screen, and wants to order lunch before first period.
And every design decision can be checked against Orla. Would this help Orla order lunch on the bus in under a minute?
A persona is also a kind of abstraction. It keeps the details that matter from lots of real people and leaves out the rest.
Next, user stories. A user story describes one thing a user wants, in one sentence. As a, I want, so that.
For example. As a pupil, I want to see a confirmation after I order, so that I know my lunch will be ready.
The so that bit is really important. It explains why the feature matters. If you can't think of a so that, maybe nobody needs it.
And to know when a story is finished, you add acceptance criteria. These are specific checks you can test with a yes or a no.
So not, the page loads fast. Instead, the menu page loads in under three seconds on a phone.
Pause and test yourself. What's wrong with this story? As a developer, I want a cloud database, so that data is stored.
It's about the technology, not about what a user wants. Users don't care what's inside. Keep stories about the user.
Now, usability principles. These are like a checklist for any app, website or game.
Consistency. Things that do the same job look and work the same everywhere. The menu stays in the same place on every page.
Feedback. Always show the user what's happening. A spinner while it loads, then, order placed, number two one four.
Otherwise you tap pay, nothing happens, you tap again, and you've paid for two lunches.
Simple navigation. Users should always know where they are, where they can go, and how to get back.
Error prevention. Make mistakes hard to make. A date picker instead of a free text box, or, are you sure you want to delete?
And speak the user's language. Say pay, not execute transaction.
Good error messages say what went wrong, and what to do next, in plain words, right next to the problem. And they never wipe what you've typed.
Next up, wireframes and prototypes. Because building a whole app and then finding out people hate it would be a disaster.
A wireframe is a simple outline of a screen. Plain boxes and labels showing where things go. No colours, no photos, no real text.
Leaving out that detail so you can focus on the layout is abstraction again.
A prototype is an early model that users can try out. Low fidelity means simple and rough, like paper sketches. High fidelity looks almost like the real thing.
Start low. It's quick and cheap, so big changes cost almost nothing. You can even run a paper prototype test, where one person plays the computer and swaps the paper screens when the tester taps.
Sketch first, polish later.
Now one of the most important parts. Accessibility.
Accessibility means designing so that everyone can use a product, including disabled people. And more than one in five people in the UK are disabled.

But it helps far more people than that. Designers think about permanent needs, like being blind, temporary needs, like a broken wrist, and situational needs, like holding a baby in one arm, or a noisy bus.
Think of dropped kerbs. Made for wheelchair users, but handy for buggies, bikes and suitcases too. That's called the kerb-cut effect.
The international standard is WCAG. That stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines, written by the W3C, the World Wide Web Consortium.
The current version is WCAG two point two. There are three levels: single A, double A, and triple A. Double A is the usual target.
And WCAG is built on four principles that spell POUR. Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust.
Perceivable. Users can see, hear or feel the content. So alt text on images, captions on videos, and good colour contrast.
Operable. Users can use every control. Everything should work with just a keyboard, using Tab, Shift Tab and Enter.
Understandable. Clear language, consistent menus and helpful error messages.
And Robust. Correct, standard code that works with lots of browsers and with assistive technology, like screen readers.
Quick numbers. For normal text, double A needs a contrast ratio of at least four point five to one. For large text, three to one.
And never rely on colour alone. About one in twelve men are colour blind. So if a dish is vegetarian, don't just colour it green. Add a V or a labelled leaf.
Pause and test yourself. Captions on a video. Which POUR principle do they mainly support?
Perceivable. They let deaf users, and anyone watching with the sound off, take in what's being said.
Inclusive design goes even wider. It means designing for the full range of people: different ages, abilities, languages, cultures, devices and internet connections.
And bias in design is when a product works well for some groups and badly for others. Usually by accident, because the designers assumed everyone is like them.
Here's a local one. Some forms reject names with a fada, like Seán, or an apostrophe, like O'Neill. They say, invalid characters.
Which is a bit much when it's your own name. The fix is simple: accept the names people actually have.
Bias can be in data too. A voice assistant trained mostly on other accents might struggle with a good strong Fermanagh accent.
The cure for bias is the same every time. Research and test with a wide range of real users.
Speaking of testing. Usability testing means watching real users try real tasks. Give them a task, watch, take notes, and don't help them.
That's the hard part. If you have to explain it, the design isn't clear enough.
In think-aloud testing, the tester says what they're thinking as they go. That tells you why they're stuck, not just where.
And you don't need hundreds of testers. About five users usually shows up most of the big problems. Fix them, then test again.
Then there's A B testing. Two versions, A and B, shown to different groups of users, and you measure which works better.
Pause and test yourself. Version B of a canteen home page had four hundred visitors and two hundred and sixty orders. What's its success rate?
Two hundred and sixty divided by four hundred, times one hundred. Sixty-five percent.
But remember, an A B test tells you which version did better, not why. For the why, you watch and listen to users.
And when you find problems, fix the most serious ones that affect the most people first. A missing pay button beats a shade of blue.
Last idea: development cycles. Software goes through planning, design, development, testing and refinement. But different approaches arrange those stages differently.
In the waterfall approach, each stage is done once, fully, in order. Analysis, design, implementation, testing, deployment. Like water flowing down steps.
It's good when the requirements are clear and won't change, like traffic light software. But users often don't see anything until near the end, when changes are expensive.
In an iterative approach you go round the cycle many times, improving each time. Agile is a popular way of doing this.
In agile, work is split into sprints, usually one to four weeks. Each sprint, the team builds the most important user stories, tests them, and shows users a working version.
And agile does not mean no planning. It means planning in smaller pieces.
Finally, the case study. A school in Enniskillen redesigns its canteen ordering website.
Research showed most pupils order on phones, pupils didn't know if orders went through, parents didn't know when the balance was low, and the menu was just a photo.
So they made personas, like Orla the pupil, Mark the parent and Bernie the canteen supervisor, and wrote user stories for each.
A paper prototype test showed three out of five pupils couldn't find the basket. So they made it a big bar along the bottom, and in the retest everyone found it.
They typed the menu as real text, added V labels, alt text, strong contrast and keyboard access, and a clear confirmation after paying.
And the result? Before, eleven out of twenty pupils managed to order. That's fifty-five percent. After, nineteen out of twenty. Ninety-five percent.
And ordering went from three minutes down to fifty seconds. Not bad at all.
So let's recap. One: user-centred design asks who a design works for, not just whether it works.
Two: find out user needs with interviews, surveys and observation, and sum them up in personas.
Three: user stories go, as a, I want, so that, with testable acceptance criteria.
Four: follow usability principles, and sketch wireframes and low-fidelity prototypes before you build.
Five: design for accessibility using WCAG and POUR, and watch out for bias.
And six: test with real users, fix the biggest problems, and keep iterating.
That's it for this episode. Now go and try the quiz at the end of each page.
And next time you push a pull door, remember. It's not you. It's the design. Thanks for listening.
